A.explanation: Derived quantities such as force in $\text{N}$ or energy in $\text{J}$ do not use a base unit alone, so a base unit is too restrictive.

B.explanation: Standard form is useful for very large or small values but is not required, for example $5.0 \text{ m}$ is fully accurate without it.

C.explanation: Every physical quantity is a numerical magnitude multiplied by a unit, for example $3.0 \text{ kg}$ or $12 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

D.explanation: Non-SI units such as $\text{cm}$, $\text{eV}$ or $\text{mmHg}$ can still accurately represent a quantity, so SI is not compulsory.

hints: Notice the word all in the question - test each statement against both base quantities like mass and derived quantities like force.
Recall that a quantity such as $20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ needs a size part and a reference part - check which options force standard form, base units only, or SI units only.
Compare a normal measurement like $2.5 \text{ cm}$ with the four wordings to see which extra condition fails while still being an accurate representation.
walkthrough: Identify what a physical quantity means: a comparison of how much of something there is with an agreed reference, written as numerical magnitude times unit.

Check the restrictive words: base in option A excludes derived units such as the newton, standard form in option B excludes ordinary numbers such as $4.2 \text{ A}$, and SI in option D excludes accepted non-SI units such as centimetre or electronvolt.
Confirm that no extra restriction is needed: any unit, base, derived or non-SI, combined with a number gives a complete and accurate value with correct dimensions.
Conclude that only a unit and a numerical magnitude are required for all cases. This is option C
